body.p: The final Office Action dated December 30, 2024, has been received and carefully noted. The above amendments to the claims, and the following remarks, are submitted as a full and complete response thereto.

Claims 1, 2, 5, 12, 15, 20, and 21 have been amended. Support for the claim amendments can be found at least in original and allowable claims 5, 15, and 21, FIGS. 9 and 12, and paragraphs [0035], [0041], [0085], and [0107] of the subject application. No claims have been cancelled. No claims have been added. No new matter is added. Claims 1-26 are currently pending in the application, of which claims 1, 12, and 20 are independent claims. Further examination and reconsideration of the application is respectfully requested.

Applicant notes with Appreciation the Office Action's indication on page 7 that claims 5- 8, 15-18, and 21-24 recite allowable subject matter. Applicant kindly thanks the Examiner for the assistance. Applicant respectfully submits that all of the claims are allowable at least in view of the following.
Unaddressed Traversal
In the previous Response, Applicant argued on pages 16 and 17 that:

Furthermore, with respect to claim 3, the claim recites, in part, that "the target platform configuration is or comprises a global scope for the RPA project that generates activities for the plurality of different target platforms automatically within a scope of the RPA workflow." Claim 13, which has its own scope, recites similar features. In rejecting these features, the Office Action, on page 4, relied on
paragraph [0011] of Weinert, Jr. et al. Applicant respectfully submits that Weinert,
Jr. et al. fails to disclose these features, both explicitly and implicitly.

Applicant respectfully submits that there is no automatic generation of activities, nor is there a mention of RPA workflows in Weinert, Jr. et al. Applicant also respectfully submits that in addition to these features not being mentioned in Weinert, Jr. et al., there is no global scope that automatically generates such activities for a plurality of different target platforms, as claimed. In Weinert, Jr. et al, one cannot develop a single RPA workflow and have it work for multiple
operating systems, for instance.
Applicant respectfully submits that similar issues also exist with respect to the other
rejected dependent claims.

However, Applicant respectfully notes that this traversal was not addressed in the outstanding Office Action. This failure to answer the substance of Applicant's arguments renders the Office Action incomplete as to all matters, as is required by 37 C.F.R. § 1.104(b). Furthermore, MPEP § 707.07(f) states that "[i]n order to provide a complete application file history and to enhance the clarity of the prosecution history record, an examiner must provide clear explanations of all actions taken by the examiner during prosecution of an application." Emphasis added. "Where the applicant traverses any rejection, the examiner should, if he or she repeats the rejection, take note of the applicant's argument and answer the substance of it." Id., emphasis added. "The examiner must address all arguments which have not already been responded to in the statement of the rejection." MPEP § 707.07(f), Examiner Note 1.

In the present case, the outstanding Office Action failed to address Applicant's traversal and arguments noted above. Failure to specifically respond to Applicant's arguments renders the Office Action arbitrary and capricious, and therefore invalid, under the Administrative Procedure Act (5 U.S.C. § 706), a standard to which all Actions by the USPTO must adhere. See Dickenson v. Zurko, 527 U.S. 150 (1999).

Applicant respectfully requests that the Examiner address the substance of Applicant's arguments in the next Office Action if a Notice of Allowance is not issued. Further, Applicant respectfully notes that at least because the outstanding Office Action is incomplete under 37 C.F.R. § 1.104(b) and does not meet the requirements of MPEP § 707.07(f), the finality of the outstanding Office Action must be withdrawn.

On pages 2-5, the Office Action rejected claims 1-4, 9-14, 19, 20, 25, and 26 under 35 U.S.C. § 102(a)(1)(1) as allegedly being anticipated by Weinert, Jr. et al. (U.S. Patent Application Publication No. 2020/0004798).

Independent claim 1 recites, in part, "(a) configur[ing] an RPA project in accordance with a target platform configuration comprising a plurality of target platforms, (b) configur[ing] multiple versions of one or more activities for the respective target platform for the respective version, or (c) both (a) and (b)." Independent claims 12 and 20, which each have their own scope, recite similar features to (a) and (b), respectively. In rejecting these features, the Office Action, on page 2, relied on paragraphs [0011]-[0016] of Weinert, Jr. et al. for (a) and on paragraph [0017] of (b). Applicant respectfully submits that Weinert, Jr. et al. fails to disclose all of the features in the rejected claims, both explicitly, and implicitly.

In the previous Response, Applicant argued that a web browser is not a target platform. Rather, the web browser is an application. In the Response to Arguments section, the Office Action, on page 5, alleged that:
Applicant alleges a web browser is not a "target platform" because the specification gives examples, albeit an open ended one, of target platforms including "legacy

targets, .NET Core, cross-platform (e.g., able to run on both Windows and Linux), Apple OS X, native mobile, and the like". Examiner, respectfully, disagrees that the claim element "target platform" under the broadest reasonable interpretation should have such a narrow interpretation. The claims do not narrow the claim element "target platform" to any of the specified platforms in the specification. It is not incumbent on the Examiner to import limitations from the specification into the claims. In this regard, Weinert discloses creating RPAs that remain vendor and
platform agnostic ([0011]).
Applicant respectfully disagrees.
While it is not incumbent on the Examiner to import limitations from the specification,
Applicant respectfully notes that it is incumbent on the Examiner to apply the broadest reasonable
interpretation (BRI) standard in accordance with Phillips and other controlling case law. Applicant
respectfully submits that the reasoning in the Office Action appears to have omitted a key portion
of the test for how claim scope is determined - namely that claim features must be accorded their
broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the specification as it would be understood by one
of ordinary skill in the art. The Federal Circuit's en banc decision in Phillips v. AWH Corp.1
expressly recognized that the USPTO employs the "broadest reasonable interpretation" standard:

The Patent and Trademark Office ("PTO") determines the scope of claims in patent applications not solely on the basis of the claim language, but upon giving claims their broadest reasonable construction "in light of the specification as it would be interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art." In re Am. Acad. of Sci. Tech. Ctr., 367 F.3d 1359, 1364[, 70 USPQ2d 1827, 1830] (Fed. Cir. 2004). Indeed, the rules of the PTO require that application claims must "conform to the invention as set forth in the remainder of the specification and the terms and phrases used in the claims must find clear support or antecedent basis in the description so that the meaning of the terms in the claims may be ascertainable by reference to the
description." 37 CFR 1.75(d)(1).2
1 See Phillips v. AWH Corp., 415 F.3d 1303, 1316 (Fed. Cir. 2005).
2 See Id.; see also In re Suitco Surface, Inc., 603 F.3d 1255, 1259 (Fed. Cir. 2010); In re Hyatt, 211 F.3d 1367, 1372 (Fed. Cir. 2000); MPEP § 2111.

The broadest reasonable interpretation does not mean the broadest possible interpretation. Rather, the meaning given to a claim term must be consistent with the ordinary and customary meaning of the term, unless the term has been given a special definition in the specification (as is the case with terms noted below), and the meaning must be consistent with the use of the claim term in the specification and drawings. Further, the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claims must be consistent with the interpretation that those skilled in the art would reach.3 Additionally, the meaning of words used in a claim is not construed in a "lexicographic vacuum, but in the context of the specification and drawings."4 In some cases, the meaning of a particular claim term may be defined by implication, i.e., according to the usage of the term in the context in the specification.5

Applicant respectfully submits that in software, a "platform" is a term known to those skilled in the art that refers to a foundational system or infrastructure that provides a base for developing and running applications, essentially acting as a common environment where different software programs can interact and function together, such as an operating system. For instance, TechTarget defines a "platform" as:

3 See In re Cortright, 165 F.3d 1353, 1359 (Fed. Cir. 1999) (The Board's construction of the claim limitation "restore hair growth" as requiring the hair to be returned to its original state was held to be an incorrect interpretation of the limitation. The court held that, consistent with applicant's disclosure and the disclosure of three patents from analogous arts using the same phrase to require only some increase in hair growth, one of ordinary skill would construe "restore hair growth" to mean that the claimed method increases the amount of hair grown on the scalp, but does not necessarily produce a full head of hair.). Thus the focus of the inquiry regarding the meaning of a claim should be what would be reasonable from the perspective of one of ordinary skill in the art. In re Suitco Surface, Inc., 603 F.3d 1255, 1260 (Fed. Cir. 2010); In re Buszard, 504 F.3d 1364 (Fed. Cir. 2007). In Buszard, the claim was directed to a flame retardant composition comprising a flexible polyurethane foam reaction mixture. 504 F.3d at 1365. The Federal Circuit found that the Board's interpretation that equated a "flexible" foam with a crushed "rigid" foam was not reasonable. Id. at 1367. Persuasive argument was presented that persons experienced in the field of polyurethane foams know that a flexible mixture is different than a rigid foam mixture. Id. at 1366.
4 See Toro Co. v. White Consolidated Industries Inc., 199 F.3d 1295, 1301 (Fed. Cir. 1999).
5 See Phillips, 415 F.3d at 1320-21; see also Vitronics Corp. v. Conceptronic Inc., 90 F.3d 1576, 1583 (Fed. Cir. 1996).

any hardware or software used to host an application or service. An application platform, for example, consists of hardware, an operating system (OS), and coordinating programs that use the instruction set for a particular processor or microprocessor. In this case, the platform creates a foundation that ensures object
code executes successfully.

See https://www.techtarget.com/searchitoperations/definition/platform. See also https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computing platform, which describes aa software platform as the infrastructure on which software is executed.

A web browser, on the other hand, is not itself a platform, but rather, a software application that functions as a tool to access and view web pages. It does not provide a foundation for developing other applications like a full-fledged platform would. See

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web browser, for example. Applicant also respectfully submits that the disclosure in paragraph [0026] of the subject application of example target platforms that include "legacy targets, .NET Core, cross-platform (e.g., able to run on both Windows® and Linux®), Apple® OS X, native mobile, and the like" provides context to the skilled person as to what a platform is, which is consistent with Toro.

It should also be noted that in the context of the claimed invention, configuration of the RPA project in accordance with a target platform configuration that includes a plurality of target platforms is not the same as being platform-agnostic. Rather, this means that the RPA project is configured to execute its steps for a given target platform based on the associated logic. As disclosed in paragraph [0027] of the subject application, for example:

Some embodiments allow multiple target platforms to be handled in the same project. The target platform(s) can be specified at the automation and/or activitySVG {EMBED HERE} 0.3670.34 in order to provide the supported functionality for each. This may also allow ously built automations to be applied to new target frameworks without
g from scratch.
Emphasis added. This differs from merely using a platform-agnostic language such as Java, for example, where the target platform is irrelevant.
In the Response to Arguments section, the Office Action, on pages 5 and 6, alleged that:

Applicant alleges that a developer can create a workflow in a project that would work for multiple target platforms. However, claim 1 does not disclose a "workflow" or a "developer". Claim 1 discloses an RPA project configured in accordance with a target platform configuration comprising a plurality of target platforms. The metes and bounds, according to the claim language, of a "project"

can include a user utilizing a designer interface to design first and second RPA applications for first and second websites. Weinert utilizes high level wrappers around specific points of robotic process automation to remain vendor and platform agnostic, i.e., specific raw coded scripts for specific platforms are not required.
This allows migration to an entirely new underlying technology utilizing the "handler" abstraction layer to design the RPA application. Therefore, Weinert does
allow developers/users to build RPA's for different platforms.

The subject application provides definitions regarding what is included in an automation project. For instance, paragraph [0035] of the subject application discloses that "[t]he automation project enables automation of rule-based processes by giving the developer control of the execution order and the relationship between a custom set of steps developed in a workflow, defined herein as 'activities."' RPA robots, on the other hand, "are execution agents that run workflows built in designer 110." See paragraph [0041] of the subject application. Applicant thus respectfully submits that an RPA workflow including activities is inherently included within the RPA project. However, purely in the interest of expediting prosecution of the subject application, Applicant has amended the independent claims to make these implicit features explicit.

With respect to the independent claims potentially including a user utilizing a designer interface (would inherently be an RPA designer application) to design first and second RPA applications for first and second websites, Applicant respectfully submits that this is partially correct. However, a user can't design RPA applications. Rather, the user can design RPA

workflows which RPA robots then execute. Also, per the above, websites and web browsers are not software platforms within the plain meaning of the term and the disclosure and context of the subject application. Furthermore, Weinert, Jr. et al. still does not allow a user to accommodate multiple target platforms in a single RPA project, as claimed. As known to those skilled in the art, this would include an RPA workflow, dependencies, etc.

Applicant also respectfully submits that features appear to have been read into Weinert, Jr. et al. that are not disclosed therein and are not implicit therefrom. Using "high level wrappers around specific points of robotic process automation to remain vendor and platform agnostic" is not the same as what is claimed. The claimed invention is not merely allowing developers to build RPAs for different platforms. Rather, as claimed, the developer can accommodate different platforms in a single RPA project.
In the Response to Arguments section, the Office Action, on page 6, alleged that:

With respect to the "configuring multiple versions ... version", the limitation is recited in the alternative and is therefore not provided patentable weight. In the interest of compact prosecution, however, the claim does not disclose what actions constitute said activities. Therefore, under the broadest reasonable interpretation, any endeavor taken with respect to the target web browser is an activity for that web browser. In Weinart, [sic] the act of determining a value for the configuration parameter for the website is an activity. This activity is interpreted as having "multiple versions". The first "version" of the activity determines a first value specific to a first user based on a first context of a first job assistance. The second "version" of the activity determines a second value specific to a second user based on a second context of a second job instance. The activity involves the determination of the value. The versions are merely interpreted as different values that are being determined. Unless the claims are narrowed to include "steps in a RPA workflows, [sic] such as clicking a button, opening a file, etc.", the Examiner
will continue to employ the broadest reasonable interpretation.
Applicant respectfully submits that the definition in paragraph [0035] of the subject application must be employed when interpreting what the claimed activities mean. Any endeavor

taken with respect to a "target" web browser is thus not an activity in the context of the claimed invention when the Phillips BRI standard is employed. Determining first and second values is not equivalent to different versions of an activity. Indeed, in Weinert, Jr. et al., it seems that the same action determines both values based on the user and context. There is not one version for one platform and another version for another platform, for example. Again, Weinert, Jr. et al. is alleged to be platform-agnostic.

Applicant has also amended the independent claims to recite the multi-target automation generation feature from allowable claims 5, 15, and 21. Applicant agrees that such features patentably distinguish over the art.
Thus, Applicant respectfully submits that the independent claims patentably distinguish over Weinert Jr. et al.

Claims 2-4, 9-11, 13, 14, 19, 25, and 26 depend from independent claim 1, 12, or 26 and inherit the patentable features thereof. At least by virtue of their dependencies, Applicant respectfully submits that claims 2-4, 9-11, 13, 14, 19, 25, and 26 also patentably distinguish over Weinert, Jr. et al.

Furthermore, with respect to claim 3, the claim recites, in part, that "the target platform configuration is or comprises a global scope for the RPA project that generates activities for the plurality of different target platforms automatically within a scope of the RPA workflow." Claim 13, which has its own scope, recites similar features. In rejecting these features, the Office Action, on page 4, relied on paragraph [0011] of Weinert, Jr. et al. Applicant respectfully submits that Weinert, Jr. et al. fails to disclose these features, both explicitly and implicitly.

Applicant respectfully submits that there is no automatic generation of activities, nor is there a mention of RPA workflows in Weinert, Jr. et al. Applicant also respectfully submits that in addition to these features not being mentioned in Weinert, Jr. et al., there is no global scope that automatically generates such activities for a plurality of different target platforms, as claimed. In Weinert, Jr. et al., one cannot develop a single RPA workflow and have it work for multiple operating systems, for instance.
Applicant respectfully submits that similar issues also exist with respect to the other rejected dependent claims.

Applicant further respectfully notes that a claim is anticipated only if each and every element as set forth in the claim is found, either expressly or inherently described, in a single prior art reference. See Verdegaal Bros. v. Union Oil Co. of California, 814 F.2d 628, 631, 2 USPQ2d 1051, 1053 (Fed. Cir. 1987), emphasis added. When a claim covers several structures or compositions, either generically or as alternatives, the claim is deemed anticipated if any of the structures or compositions within the scope of the claim is known in the prior art. See Brown v. 3M, 265 F.3d 1349, 1351, 60 USPQ2d 1375, 1376 (Fed. Cir. 2001). The identical invention must be shown in as complete detail as is contained in the claim. See Richardson v. Suzuki Motor Co., 868 F.2d 1226, 1236, 9 USPQ2d 1913, 1920 (Fed. Cir. 1989), emphasis added. The claimed features discussed above are missing from Weinert, Jr. et al., and furthermore, the features are not presented in as complete detail as claimed. As such, Applicant respectfully submits that Weinert, Jr. et al. explicitly cannot anticipate all of the features recited in the rejected claims.
Accordingly, Applicant respectfully submits that the rejection has been overcome and respectfully requests that the rejection be withdrawn.
CONCLUSION

In view of the above, Applicant respectfully submits that the present application is in condition for allowance. Accordingly, Applicant respectfully requests that the claims be allowed and the application be passed to issue.

Although Applicant has focused the remarks and/or amendments on or primarily on the independent claims in order to expedite the prosecution of the instant application, Applicant reserves the right to remark on and/or amend any of the dependent claims at any time. The mere fact that Applicant has not remarked on and/or amended any of the dependent claims at this time, either related to an Official Notice or not, is unequivocally not an admission of prior art.

Although the present communication may include alterations to the application or claims, or characterizations of claim scope or referenced art, Applicant is not conceding in this application that previously pending claims are not patentable over the cited references. Rather, any alterations or characterizations are being made to facilitate expeditious prosecution of this application.

Applicant reserves the right to pursue at a later date any previously pending or other broader or narrower claims that capture any subject matter supported by the present disclosure, including subject matter found to be specifically disclaimed herein or by any prior prosecution.

Accordingly, reviewers of this or any parent, child or related prosecution history shall not reasonably infer that Applicant has made any disclaimers or disavowals of any subject matter supported by the present application.
If for any reason the Examiner determines that the application is not now in condition for allowance, it is respectfully requested that the Examiner contact, by telephone, Applicant's
undersigned representative at the indicated telephone number to arrange for an interview to
expedite the disposition of this application.
In the event this paper is not being timely filed, Applicant respectfully petitions for an
appropriate extension of time. Any fees for such an extension together with any additional fees
may be charged to Counsel's Deposit Account 50-5837.
